## The last step is a whole tone, and that's the problem

Play the white notes from A up to A and pay attention to the final step. G to A
is a whole tone. Compare it with B to C at the top of a major scale, where the
semitone shoves you into the tonic, and you'll hear what's missing: the arrival
happens, but nothing pushed it. Composers wanted that push back. So they raised
the seventh degree when they needed it, which is why minor comes to you as a
family of related forms and not as one settled row of notes.

Three members show up constantly. *Natural minor* rotates the major pattern to
start on degree 6. *Harmonic minor* raises degree 7 in both directions, manufacturing
a leading tone. *Melodic minor* raises degrees 6 and 7 on the way up, then drops
back to natural minor coming down. Presented as three lists of note names,
they look like trivia to memorise. Line up the arrays and you can see what each
edit is for: one builds a semitone approach to the tonic, and the second removes
the hole the first one left behind.

## Three forms and one tune to test them with

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 108
use_synth :piano

define :play_phrase do |notes|
  notes.each do |pitch|
    play pitch, release: 0.35
    sleep 0.5
  end
end

natural = [57, 59, 60, 62, 64, 65, 67, 69]
harmonic = [57, 59, 60, 62, 64, 65, 68, 69]
melodic_up = [57, 59, 60, 62, 64, 66, 68, 69]
melodic_down = natural.reverse

puts "harmonic changes: #{natural.zip(harmonic).select { |a, b| a != b }}"
puts "melodic changes: #{natural.zip(melodic_up).select { |a, b| a != b }}"

[natural, harmonic, melodic_up].each do |notes|
  play_phrase notes
  play_phrase notes.reverse
  sleep 1
end

play_phrase melodic_up + melodic_down.drop(1)

tune_degrees = [0, 2, 4, 3, 2, 5, 6, 7, 4, 3, 2, 1, 6, 7, 0]
[natural, harmonic, melodic_up].each do |scale_notes|
  play_phrase tune_degrees.map { |degree| scale_notes[degree] }
  sleep 1
end
```

The diff in the log is tiny: one changed position for harmonic, two for melodic.
Your ears get something much less tiny. Harmonic minor opens a three-semitone
gap between F and G-sharp, then closes hard from G-sharp to A. Melodic minor
lifts F to F-sharp on the ascent and the gap flattens out into ordinary steps.
Then the same fifteen-degree tune runs through all three. Which of the three
do you expect to end most like a finished cadence, and which one actually did?

## Alter the alteration

1. Lower harmonic minor's G-sharp back to G in the last two notes only, leaving
   the earlier alterations alone. The scale keeps its colour and loses its
   cadence. That split is the point of the exercise.
2. Swap `:piano` for `:prophet` and set `release: 0.8`. Now F and G-sharp overlap
   in the air, and the wide interval becomes something you hear rather than
   something you read out of a diff.
3. Add 5 to every pitch in every array. The whole family moves from A to D and
   the differences between the three forms survive intact.

## Two edits, two different jobs

Natural minor starts on degree 6 of its relative major, so rotating the major
formula gives you `2, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2, 2`. Its seventh degree lands two semitones
under the tonic. Raise it and the closing interval contracts to a semitone,
which is precisely the pull major gets for free.

That fix creates a fresh problem one degree lower. Natural degree 6 and raised
degree 7 now sit three semitones apart. Harmony can exploit that gap; a rising
melodic line doesn't cross it comfortably. Melodic minor raises degree 6 as well, so
degrees 5, 6 and 7 become even whole tones. Coming down, degree 7 has nothing
above it to press into, so the natural form returns without fighting anything.

Keeping all three forms as data does real work here. `zip` lines the positions
up, `select` reports the ones that differ, and the tune consumes whatever
eight-note array you hand it. You get to hear the scale choice against a fixed
melodic design, and the explanation stays next to the numbers responsible for
the sound.

## Generate the family from formulas

Write `minor_forms(root)` returning a hash with `:natural`, `:harmonic`,
`:melodic_up` and `:melodic_down`. Build each one from a step formula; don't
paste note lists. Before you listen, assert that natural and harmonic differ at
exactly one index, and that natural and melodic-up differ at exactly two.

Then play a two-octave E-minor line, ascending through the melodic form and
descending through the natural one. The assertions protect the family
resemblance. The playback tells you what those one or two changed integers
actually do to a phrase.
